newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Clarke helps soothe Conservative jitters.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Clarke helps soothe Conservative jitters.

text.p: Finance Minister Kenneth Clarke's one point cut in income tax in his budget on Tuesday helped soothe the fears of Conservative members of parliament worried about their prospects in Britain's looming general election.

But members of the ruling party, concerned that Prime Minister John Major has been unable to reverse the opposition Labour party's consistent poll lead, believe the budget alone will not be enough to win them an unprecedented fifth term in office.

Walter Sweeney, an endangered Conservative MP who won his Vale of Glamorgan seat in Wales by a hair-breadth 19 votes at the last election, told Reuters: "I think it's a sound budget and it reverts to our tax cutting traditions...

"It's not going to win us the election on its own but I think it's consistent with what we need to be doing to impress the electorate with our economic competence and our desire to get taxes down," Sweeney said.
Others were more upbeat about the package, whose cornerstone was a cut in basic income tax to 23 percent from 24 percent.

David Shaw, Conservative MP for Dover, and a member of the House of Commons Treasury Committee, told Reuters: "It is an excellent budget, enormously prudent. It should go down well in the constituencies as well as in the City of London.
Another Conservative on the panel, Quentin Davies, said it was a sound, responsible budget typical of Clarke and would go down well with voters.
"It was a splendid budget -- just what we wanted. Ken didn't give in to the slightest degree to the temptation to go for any kind of electoral gimmick," Davies told Reuters.
"He believes -- and I'm sure he's right -- that at general elections one gets credit for one's record over time and for the seriousness and soundness of one's policies," he added.

However, one Eurosceptic MP opposed to moves towards European integration -- on the opposite wing of the party from Europhile Clarke -- was less enthusiastic, saying the budget lacked any big giveaway to tempt voters.
The MP was also irked by a Clarke jibe at the Eurosceptics' expense when he stressed the budget would allow Britain to meet the Maastricht criteria for joining a European single currency.
Clarke was forced on Monday to make a rare eve-of-budget statement to defuse a row over parliamentary scrutiny of European Union rules governing the single currency.

Labour and the minority Liberal Democrats were predictably scathing about the budget, saying figures released alongside his speech show taxes will actually go up and spending on health and education fall -- after the election.
